en: The Secret Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Forty-eight Messengers of the Vidyārāja Acala Vijayabhaṭa, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery.
At that time, by imperial decree, the Indian Brahmin monk Vidyākara gathered [the assembly], and the Bodhisattva Prajñā entered the samādhi known as the "Vajra Attainment."
Blazing with fierce flames,
its fire illuminated all buddha-fields and completely incinerated the trichiliocosm.
All the Māras who create obstacles therein, as well as all the Vināyakas,
Rākṣasas, and so forth, shall be completely overwhelmed by this great fire,
which burns with the agony of pestilence.
The limbs suffer from agonizing pain that twists and constricts the body;
the mind becomes bewildered and faints, and all cry out in loud voices.
When worldly people encounter the pressure of great suffering, they utter cries of "Mi-mi."
The sound filled the trichiliocosm;
all sentient beings who heard this sound were utterly terrified and fled in all directions.
As they prostrated before the Buddha, they all spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, we now take refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi held [the vajra].
Rising from samādhi, he addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
"How is it that you see the various celestial lords, Śakras, and others arriving here?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva then spoke to Vajrapāṇi.
"I cannot know this;
only a Tathāgata knows it.
Having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
The two great beings then remained silent.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi again addressed Mañjuśrī:
"The Wrathful King named Noble Vijaya-acala is the Vidyārāja Acala."
I shall now explain this mind and the secret mudrā.
Therefore, all you members of the great assembly, Vajrasattva Bodhisattvas,
and sons of noble family, listen attentively!
Possessing boundless power and valor,
he is the immovable Great Fierce Wrathful King who performs the infinite deeds of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, there are eighty trillion *koṭi* of Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All have received his instructions and teachings, thereby attaining unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable devas, nāgas,
and the eight classes of beings who constantly and perpetually make offerings, pay homage, and serve him.
If one merely recollects this King of Wrathful Power,
it can cause all obstacles and difficulties to be entirely severed and destroyed;
no obstacle or difficulty will dare to approach.
One should always remain far removed from such places.
This is the dwelling place of practitioners,
where there are no demonic activities or calamities caused by various spirits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva arose from his samādhi and summoned all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
All classes of sentient beings gathered there,
he further extracted and synthesized their diverse mentalities,
causing them to become one body and abide equally in samādhi.
The conflagrations that burn many koṭis of worlds are extinguished,
becoming a single great mass of fire,
like the light of seven suns illuminating the mouth of the Great Horse (*Mahāśva*) and other such places.
All flowing streams are swallowed and absorbed without remainder, entirely becoming fierce flames.
This is the recitation of the subtle heart-mantra of the Great Wrathful King, the Invincible Vajra-Hūṃkāra;
it is also the great horse’s mouth that devours all sentient beings.
The various karmas, afflictions, and mental causes of all sentient beings together constitute the world of great blazing flames.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prajñā addressed the Buddha, saying:
I, along with all Tathāgatas, all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and even the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas— all sentient beings within the realm of living beings.
Out of a desire to show compassion, transform, and benefit [beings],
the Vidyārāja Vijaya manifests in a wrathful form,
emerging from the heart of Mahāvairocana as one of the five Vidyārājas.
All Buddhas are thus.
This is the fivefold gate of the pāramitās of the Five Vidyārājas of Mahāvairocana,
and it further gives birth to their emanations.
The first vidyārāja is named Acala-vijaya.
Within the trichiliocosm, he manifests a body of sovereign flaming brilliance and majestic virtue;
he is the Prajñā Bodhisattva of the svabhāva-cakra-body.
It is for the sake of subduing and gathering sentient beings according to their respective types;
it serves as a staff for the Vajradhara disciple;
and it is for the sake of empowering his retinue to crush all obstacles.
Just as Anubhaṭa, by means of his great power, revealed the essence of the Wrathful Vajra and dwelt in the samādhi of Fire-Born,
he spoke the mantra for the Destroyer of Great Obstacles.
This mantra possesses great majesty and power; it can eliminate all things,
crush obstacles and difficulties for the practitioner,
and protect and increase [virtue] from the moment the bodhicitta is generated.
They will attain the fruit of Buddhahood in its entirety;
they shall never regress or fall into non-pathways,
and shall swiftly realize the fruit within the Buddha-way itself.
The Four Great Vows of the Vidyārāja state:
"May those who see my body awaken the bodhicitta;
may those who hear my name sever evil and cultivate goodness; may those who hear me speak attain great wisdom."
One who knows my heart attains Buddhahood in this very body;
by once holding this secret mantra,
they shall receive protection throughout every lifetime.
Those who maintain mindfulness of me shall not fall into doubt,
let alone encounter the various obstacles of the world;
there are only two such [obstacles].
The first is internal obstruction,
which arises from one's own mind;
its varieties are so numerous that they cannot be fully described.
Second are external obstacles,
which arise from external matters;
their types are likewise numerous.
These mantras are all capable of crushing and expelling [obstacles],
rendering the body stainless and pure;
according to the teaching, one attains Buddhahood in this very body.
This is the most secret of the profound and esoteric teachings.
What are the four kinds of causal conditions?
First is fasting.
Second is the practice of ingesting vital breath;
third is the practice of eating vegetables;
fourth is the practice of moderation in eating.
Having performed what can be accomplished according to one's capacity and having bound oneself by means of one's own body,
one should recite the root dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times, or even up to three hundred thousand times.
For one day and one night, he shall not drink water.
He shall perform extensive offerings and adorn the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
Before the painted image, he shall burn *kṛtavedhuka* wood.
Take sticks as long as a thumb, twelve finger-widths in length,
with both ends smeared with ghee and honey;
recite the mantra once for each stick and burn one stick at a time.
When one thousand and eight recitations have been completed and burned,
even minor worldly matters will be fulfilled according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, once the count of recitations has been completed:
Entering a river, a stream, or the ocean,
one should face east at a depth reaching the neck;
having recited [the mantra] for a full three lakṣas every day, [the practice is complete].
The fields of merit within one's heart shall all fulfill their vows;
even water brought to the place where snakes and turtles dwell [is thus empowered],
let alone that which has not yet been perfected through mantras and is constantly subject to damage by others— this must always be bound with a protective boundary (sīmābandha).
If one constantly applies effort in reciting the Fundamental Unmoving Mantra,
one will be able to bind all ghosts and spirits with one's own body according to one's capacity,
and can likewise hew down and cut all trees.
It can also cause birds flying in the sky to fall down before one;
it can even seize and dry up the depths of the nāgas.
If one wishes to engage in debate or to refute non-Buddhists, evildoers, and the like, [this mantra shall be employed].
"One who is able to subdue them all.
Furthermore, first wait until the moon is about to eclipse;
have [the practitioner] recite the mantra for the full number of times and drink it first.
Fasting for one day and one night,
he took cow dung that had not yet fallen to the ground.
Receive it with a vessel so that it does not reach the ground.
Second, even when it falls to the ground, ensure that dust or soil has not yet defiled it;
pick it up and place it so that it does not touch the ground again.
At the ritual altar, take various kinds of flowers and scatter them as an offering.
Take the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and place it at the center.
Take the milk from an old calf of the same color as [the practitioner] and a brown cow, and offer it as curd.
Next, take ghee and place it in a vessel made of refined copper;
stir the ghee with a ladle made of khadira wood.
At the beginning of the lunar month, drink it while reciting the mantra.
One sees up to three signs,
namely those such as the "blaze" and so forth.
As for the sign of warmth (*ūṣmagata*), if one administers it, all diseases are cured.
One who attains the sign of smoke may smear it upon their own body to remain concealed,
so that evil persons cannot see them.
One who attains the sign of the flame of fire may wear it, whereby they will possess supernatural powers and be able to fly through the air.
This refers to the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).
Regarding "the milk of an old calf":
when a calf has been born for more than a year, it becomes as large as its mother.
Yet it still eats and drinks alone;
the calf's coat must be the same color as its mother's.
In this way, the cow's milk is processed to produce ghee.
Furthermore, the practitioner should go to the summit of a high mountain,
abstain from grains and food,
and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Maintain the continuity of mind-moment to mind-moment without allowing other conditions to intervene.
Then the celestial treasure-trove will manifest spontaneously.
Generally, such treasure-troves may be of celestial origin, divine origin, or human origin.
That which is buried by people is called a "human treasure";
that which is guarded by spirits and deities is called a "divine hidden treasure," and is also termed a "terrestrial hidden treasure."
If even those protected by the various devas— who are like celestial treasures—
can still perceive it,
how much more so for one who guards and preserves a human treasure with joy?
One should perform meritorious deeds and use [the mantra] as one wishes.
Furthermore, if one recites the mantra one thousand times while burning [incense],
it can eliminate great epidemics within the kingdom.
Regarding the homa ritual:
for those who construct a hearth in the ground, one kindles the fire until it blazes.
As for the method for the ladle, it should be carved from hard wood.
The head was like a ladle, capable of holding the yolk of a chicken egg;
its tip was bright and its length was about two chi.
He then used a separate clean vessel to hold the milk.
Using this ladle to draw [the water] and recite the mantra over it,
the epidemic in the country will be cured; or,
by holding one *jita* (a measure) at home, [the same shall occur].
All mutual attachments and defilements shall be completely extinguished.
This will enable one to eliminate whatever disturbances arise in the regions of Wu, Shu, and Lingnan.
Furthermore, take the flowers of the *xiangcao* plant and mix them with ghee and honey.
Reciting the mantra once and burning [the offering] once, the robes sought will attain such colors as these flowers; all shall accord with one's wishes.
If seeking crimson, one should burn red flowers.
The rest should all be understood according to this principle.
The inconceivable power of spiritual efficacy fulfills the practitioner’s vows;
it is a measurable portion when defined by specific phenomena.
Yet the two slips of bamboo contained no inscription;
had he taken them by force or through improper means, the spirit would have treated him with contempt,
and even if he had obtained them, they would not have been valued.
If one burns one hundred thousand *lakṣas* of *mīlāva* wood,
and performs two recitations, one shall obtain the highest official rank in the kingdom;
whatever one undertakes with solemnity will surely be fulfilled.
The *mīravā* is a round fruit from outside [the region].
Furthermore, by burning *piṅgala*, *matsyākṣa*, and *saṃjñaka* flowers,
one gains the affection and joy of all people.
Burn pine wood, kindling it with the three substances;
if one does this even once, one will obtain immeasurable followers.
Burn the pine wood, which should be seven inches long and as thick as a mother’s thumb.
By reciting this mantra over barley, one attains the wealth and nobility of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
This refers to barley and black barley that still have their husks.
Regarding the method for painting the image, it is used for subduing others.
If one wishes to perform the rite, one should face the image.
With the mind focused on an object of perception, one should visualize it;
on a fine silk cloth, one should paint the Immovable Wrathful King (Acala).
He wears a crimson robe draped diagonally across his waist;
his loincloth is also crimson.
A single lock of hair on the left side hangs down as far as his ear.
The left eye gazes slightly askance;
the left hand grasps a noose,
while the right hand holds a sword held upright.
The hilt of the sword is shaped like a lotus petal;
the sword-boots are inlaid with jewels upon which curved brows frown in wrath.
One’s own form is reddish-yellow and wrathful,
appearing so as to strike fear into all sentient beings.
Having painted this image, one should stay on a seashore, in a pure *āraṇya*, or within a clean house.
The practitioner, with a purified body, shall wear red garments and visualize their own entire body as being red.
Without distraction, they shall silently beg for alms.
Once five hundred thousand recitations have been completed,
take ten thousand stalks, each five inches long,
made of three substances, and burn them before this image with a sincere mind while continuing the recitation.
The Victorious Army, Acala Vidyārāja, manifests his own body so that the practitioner may see him;
having seen him, one immediately attains the mind of the Tathāgata’s samādhi.
One shall come to dwell together with all the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, before this painted image,
one should recite the root mantra three times each day.
If one makes offerings of flowers, incense, food, and drink according to one's means for six months,
all various aspirations will be fulfilled.
Furthermore, should any robbers come, [they shall not cause harm].
If the practitioner holds one [of these items] in hand and recites [the mantra] one thousand times,
then should [an enemy] approach, those hostile bandits and the like will naturally retreat and flee.
They shall flee in all directions.
If one encounters those who are enemies of the Buddha’s Dharma or wicked persons,
one should fashion their effigies by mixing salt and earth.
Write one's name upon it.
The figure should be one cubit in length;
recite the mantra over it, and for each repetition, cut off one piece and burn it.
Even down to the burning mantra:
by reciting the name of an evil person even once,
that person is completely consumed.
If one does not subdue it, death will surely follow immediately.
Furthermore, take *mandāra* leaves and burn them;
for each incantation, recite the name of the evil person while burning them.
If one recites it one thousand times,
the person before will certainly lose their mind; however,
if one takes cow’s milk and burns it one thousand times, they will be restored to normalcy.
If one burns salt while reciting the name [of the deity],
chanting once for each burn until it is completed one thousand times,
all people within a thousand li will come to receive [one].
Burn agalloch incense,
maintaining it continuously throughout the three periods of the day;
thus one will attain the middle and superior grades of accomplishment.
The aforementioned methods above are all employed for accomplishment beneath this painted image.
In the visualization of the maṇḍala within the practice site, there is Mount Sumeru.
Above is a red lotus flower;
upon the lotus flower is a pavilion,
within which is a crystal stone.
Within the syllable *śeṣa* is the character *han*.
When this character transforms, it becomes the Venerable Acala Vijaya;
he is the wrathful manifestation of the Bodhisattva Dharmacakra-pravartaka.
"Victorious Army" (Jina) signifies mastery;
"Immovable" (Acala) signifies the bodhi of great tranquil concentration.
This is the venerable Vairocana’s body of differentiated wisdom.
Acala is an emanation of the primordial Buddha Vairocana;
after once holding this secret mantra,
he provides protection for those in the world throughout their successive lives.
If worldly habits have not yet been severed,
even if a youth has committed various worldly transgressions a thousand times,
they are all permitted to perform repentance.
He does not immediately cast them off from his front or back.
The single hair hanging down to the left represents the downward extension of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The sword held in his right hand signifies the meaning of *ājñā* (supreme knowledge).
The left hand holding a noose signifies binding; sitting upon a lotus pedestal signifies immovability.
The flames issuing from one's own body signify abiding in the samādhi of the Great Fire Wisdom-fire.
He is served by infinite Tathāgatas;
this Honored One is reverently attended by the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others.
If one merely recollects this King of Wrathful Power, [the results will follow].
All obstacles are completely severed and destroyed.
All accomplishments (*siddhi*) sought in both the mundane and supramundane realms are brought to fulfillment.
[This is] the seal-gesture (*mudrā*).
The two palms are crossed within,
with each wheel like a ring;
the two thumbs rest beside the water.
The fire-peak stands facing the void;
the two winds join together vertically.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samanta-vajra-śatru-ṭha amogha-ghāṇa-mahā-ghasana-sphoṭaya hūṃ trāmaya trāmaya hūṃ ṭha haṃ kham. [The practitioner] every day...
By reciting this mantra,
all sought-after siddhis will be accomplished.
Next is the concise method for arranging the syllables of the Noble Acala.

Oṃ at the crown of the head, its color like space; vaḥ between the eyebrows, its color like fire; ra (raḥ) on the two shoulders, its color like fire; aḥ at the heart, its color like milk; and the syllable for the circular eyes placed upon the throat, its color like the moon or gold—these five syllables are established and arrayed upon the body of the practitioner.
Within that, the syllable A contains all five syllables;
having been distributed therein, it pervades the entire body.
Therefore, one contemplates the immovable vajra-body.
Having spread it out, one should immediately recite the One-Syllable Mantra for all purposes:
*Namo samanta-vajrāya śaṃ*. Next, perform the protection of the body and the binding of the boundary.
Rest the three fingers from the middle finger downward of the left hand upon the three fingers from the middle finger downward of the right hand;
then, with the thumbs of both hands,
pinch the ring fingers.
Having finished the mutual support, straighten the index finger of the right hand and bend the index finger of the left hand;
press the second phalanx of the right index finger against the lips.
Recite the root mantra seven times.
Circumambulate three times clockwise above the crown of the head; according to the distance and range of one's intention, the entire dharma-realm shall become inviolable.
Next, enter the Buddha-samaya-mudrā.
Second is the mudrā of turning away stinginess:
join the palms with the fingers slightly apart;
place the seal upon the forehead, the right and left shoulders, the heart, and the throat.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, āsme trāsme samaye svāhā. Next is the mudrā of the Arising from the Dharmadhātu.
Form two vajra fists with the backs joined together;
extend the tips of the two index fingers so they touch,
and direct the mudrā toward the heart.
Three times.
*Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ dharma-dhātu-svabhāva-ātmaka*. Next, for the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma:
the two hands are turned back-to-back.
Interlace the earth, water, fire, and wind [fingers].
Place the two space-fingers within the palms with their tips joined.
Then, assign them to the heart and raise them three times.
The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samanta-vajrāya vajra-tattva-guhya*. Next is the Seal of Intolerance (*asahana-mudrā*).
With an open mind, join the palms with the two fire fingers interlaced;
place the two water fingers and the two wind fingers each in their respective positions.
Perform this seal over heaven and earth three times, both in the reverse and the natural order.
Seal the five places of the body and then release them at the crown of the head;
likewise, perform the boundary-binding for the four directions with the mantra.

Oṃ sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhānavajrasaṃgraha hūṃ jjaḥ svāhā. This is the mantra for the Universal Gathering of the Immovable One’s Compassionate Rescue. Namo samantavajra-krodha-mahāroṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ trāṭ haṃ khaṃ. Next is the arghya mudrā.
Place both hands palms upward.
Insert both thumbs into the palms.
Place the tips of both index fingers upon the middle joints of the thumbs.
This is the śaṅkha-mudrā.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ gaganasamāsama svāhā. Next, perform the flower-seat mudrā.
The ten wheels shall be opened and blossomed;
by means of this, one should offer them at the three locations.
Next is the mudrā and mantra of the unguent.
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ viśodhana-dhūpana-vaśa-ha.* Next is the flower-garland mudrā:
using the previous incense mudrā, place the two thumbs against the side of the ring fingers at the lower joint.
This is the mudrā for offering named flowers. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mahāmaitrīyapūjite svāhā*. Next is the incense-offering mudrā.
The two hands form the *tripuṭa* mudrā;
the earth and water fingers are extended upward,
while the two wind fingers are bent to support the upper joints.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātvanugate svāhā. Next is the seal for food and drink.
With both hands hollowed and joined in *añjali*, enter into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with wisdom. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, arara karara marinda namo marinda me mahāmarīce svāhā*. Next is the Lamp-Brightness Seal (*dīpaprabhāmudrā*).
Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ tathāgata-rājī-spharaṇa-nāga-gāminaye svāhā. This is the mantra of the Seal for Universal Offering to Space.
Oṃ Ākāśasvabhāvaśuddha. Next follows the praise of Acala:
I prostrate to the Noble Acala, The Great Fierce King of supreme compassion, Who takes pity upon all sentient beings.
The essential body is Vairocana; Entering the distant state, he attains perfect enlightenment.
The Dharma-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm; His wisdom is equal to empty space.
Though soundless, there is sound; That sound reaches through lands as numerous as motes of dust.
To uphold and protect the Buddha-dharma, And to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings,
You manifest this body through skillful means With the appearance of wrathful transformation; Therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to you.
Beholding all sentient beings with eyes of loving-kindness, equalizing them as if they were one's only child;
you extend a single strand of hair as a skillful means to indicate the ultimate truth—
homage to you, whose vajra-wisdom can sever all bonds.
The various afflictions are difficult to sever; by grasping this sharp sword, one cuts them all away without remainder.
Therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to the Vajra-samādhi, which can bind that which is difficult to bind—the fetters of karma and their habitual tendencies.
Wielding the golden noose, you bind all so that none can move;
ultimately devouring them all, you manifest the garuḍa-flame against the poisonous dragon of afflictions.
Therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to you.
You burn away the ocean of karmic obscurations;
you are able to protect the bodhicitta and cause the practitioner to dwell steadfastly.
Because you abide upon the vajra seat, I prostrate to you in homage. Even if the three realms were filled—
Because the powerful yakṣas and vidyārājas have all been subdued by you,
I prostrate and pay homage to you. Even if māras from throughout the triple world should come to harass a practitioner, you cause them to enter the path of liberation.
Therefore, I prostrate in homage; you who hold the secret mantra,
grant protection in every birth, and cause me to realize great bodhi—
therefore, I prostrate in homage to you who follow my body day and night.
The Vidyārāja is never for a moment left; one must ascend to the realm of the Flower Treasury (Sukhāvatī).
Moment by moment, one maintains the Vidyārāja, so that from lifetime to lifetime it is never forgotten.
Therefore, I prostrate with these three karmas.
The virtues of the Vidyārāja are excellent; he impartially bestows [benefits] upon all sentient beings so that they may together realize the Immovable Honored One (Acala).
By the power of my merit, by the power of the Vidyārāja’s empowerment, and by the power of the Dharma-realm—
The Ground of Immovable Sameness; I pray that the Vajra Secret Mantra, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, May empower my three secrets.
I prostrate to the power of the Vidyārāja, And may I attain the fulfillment of *siddhi*.
I prostrate to the power of the Vidyārāja, who causes the Dharma to abide long in the world.
May all sentient beings within the oceans of boundless worlds— both in my own realm and in the realms of others—
equally realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
The first, the Naga King Kurikara, is a transformation of Acala Vidyārāja in the form of one swallowing a sword.
He stands upon a flat rock.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ kuli-kāya-kāra-ja-miṅga-śānye svāhā. This is the second Gandharva Yakṣa King, an emanation of Akṣobhya Buddha, who holds a *ḍamaru* drum in his right hand.
The left hand rests upon the waist;
the eyes are wrathful,
and the fangs protrude from both the upper and lower jaws.
The color is blue.
If a person desires to obtain an official position and calls upon a messenger,
they should invoke the third Great Brahmā King, Śikhin.
Upon this flower, the Buddha’s transformation body appears, holding a spear in his right hand and pressing his left hand against his waist;
he has the form of a heavenly king and is red in color.
If a person wishes to seek wealth and nobility, they should summon the messengers:
on the fourth and seventh days, the five yakṣa kings of the Mothers,
who are emanations of Amitābha from the western quarter, holding alms bowls at his right and left.
The form of veneration;
the form of the color red.
If a person desires to obtain respect and love, they should invoke the messenger.
In the fifth [section], there are various Great Brahmā Kings of the First Dhyāna.
In the north is Amoghasiddhi’s transformation body, holding an arrow in his right hand and a bow in his left.
He stands upon a stone;
his form is black,
and his eyes have an expression of wrath.
If there is a person who wishes to attain the wisdom of liberation, they should summon the Messenger,
the Great Vidyārāja of the sixth, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
This is an emanation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, holding a staff in his right hand and resting his left hand upon his hip.
He has red hair that stands upright.
If a person wishes to obtain all their desires, they should summon this messenger.
He is the king of each of the thirty-three heavens of the seventh [heaven].
This is the emanated body of Mañjuśrī: his right hand holds a great sword, his left hand rests upon his hip, and he is black in appearance.
If a person wishes to attain great wisdom, they should invoke this messenger.
The eighth is the Heavenly King Akaniṣṭha.
He is a transformation body of Avalokiteśvara, holding a mendicant’s staff in his right hand and pressing his left hand against his waist;
he is red in color.
If a person wishes to be loved and remembered by kings and ministers, they should summon the messenger, the ninth yakṣa, Aṅkuśadhararāja.
This is a transformation body of Maitreya; his right hand holds a hook, and his left fist rests upon his waist.
It is red in form.
If a person wishes to obtain a queen or a court lady, they should summon this messenger.
